title: Microbial GAIN domains undergo autoproteolysis and enable release of diverse cell-surface-associated proteins
authors: Anna P. Brogan, David Z. Rudner
abstract: Brogan and Rudner report the identification of a microbial autoproteolytic domain that is structurally homologous to the GAIN domain of eukaryotic adhesion GPCRs. Rather than participating in transmembrane signaling, these domains tether diverse domains to the cell surface and are proposed to releas…

title: The E3 ubiquitin ligase LOP1 targets PIF4 to control plant morphogenesis
authors: Zhaoqing Song, Fengyue Zhao, Yeting Bian, Jie Dong, Dongqing Xu
abstract: Plant architecture is regulated by multiple cues. Song et al. reveal a phyB-LOP1-PIF4 module coordinating morphogenic development. phyB and LOP1 mutually stabilize each other, while LOP1 mediates PIF4 ubiquitination and degradation. Conversely, PIF4 directly binds the LOP1 promoter to activate its t…

authors: Zélie Lesterps, William Buhian, Anne-Laure Fuchs, Carole Laffont, Céline Remblière, Jean Keller, Fabienne Maillet, Pablo Portola, Isabelle Mila, Marie Françoise Jardinaud, Pierre-Marc Delaux, Julien Pirrello, Guilhem Reyt, Sandra Bensmihen

Nod factors induce the local production of auxin and engage an Aux/IAA7-ARF auxin signaling module in pericycle cells. This signaling module is shared across pla…

title: Coherent oscillations across the human brain, spinal cord, and muscle network
authors: Meaghan E. Spedden, Maike Schmidt, George C. O’Neill, Timothy O. West, Stephanie Mellor, Tim M. Tierney, Nicholas A. Alexander, Sahitya Puvvada, Martina F. Callaghan, Simon F. Farmer, Sven Bestmann, Gareth R. Barnes
abstract: Spedden et al. use optically pumped magnetometers to record magnetic fields from the human brain and spinal cord at the same time. Coherent 10–35 Hz activity links the sensorimotor cortex, cervical spinal cord, and hand muscle. The coupling is bidirectional, and the cord does not act as a passive re…

title: Ancestral karyotype reconstruction provides insights into stepwise chromosome evolution and bract coloration in the banana family
authors: Ning Fu, Pengchuan Sun, Xin Liu, Tong-Jian Liu, Yi-Bing Wang, Wei-Ming Li, Tian-Wen Xiao, Mei-Ling Chen, Xiao-Nan Li, Yong-Yuan Mi, Zheng-Feng Wang, Mathieu Rouard, Xue-Jun Ge, Hui-Run Huang, Xin-Feng Wang
abstract: Fu et al. reconstruct the ancestral karyotype of the banana family and reveal stepwise chromosome evolution through lineage-specific rearrangements. They show that breakpoint-associated regions are enriched with anthocyanin-related genes and transcription factors, providing insights into the potenti…

title: How snake embryos coil
authors: Alexandra Weber, Gillian Watson, Alexis Arvanitis-Vigneault, Kaitlyn Mesa, Charnesha E. Williams, Nicolas Di-Poï, Raul E. Diaz, Tetsuto Miyashita
abstract: Snake embryos coil, but how and why they corkscrew remains unexplored. Weber et al. find that the embryos wind up clockwise via buckling of the rapidly elongating axial body against the slow-growing, physically decoupled gut. The embryos reposition themselves in late stages, and coiling orientations…

title: Unique neural activity states predict action selection in response to visual threat
authors: Ilana Zucker-Scharff, Bella E. Brezovec, Yukun A. Hao, Yandan Wang, Minseung Choi, Sharon J. Su, Thomas R. Clandinin
abstract: Using two-photon imaging in behaving fruit flies, we find that visual threat evokes distinct behavioral responses associated with characteristic brain-wide changes in neural activity. Action selection is biased by unique neural activity patterns prior to stimulus presentation, with signals in a regi…

title: Control of water excretion in Hydra vulgaris by neural integration
authors: Wataru Yamamoto, Rafael Yuste
abstract: Hydra is one of the few cnidarians adapted to freshwater. Yamamoto and Yuste show that, to survive, it periodically expels accumulated gastric water. An endodermal neural ensemble integrates its activity until it reaches a threshold that triggers excretion via GLWamide signaling.

title: Convergent olfactory circuits for courtship in Drosophila revealed by the circuit-tracing tool ds-Tango
authors: John D. Fisher, Anthony M. Crown, Altar Sorkaç, Rareș A. Moșneanu, Sasha Martinez-Machado, Nathaniel J. Snell, Neel Vishwanath, Silas Monje, An Vo, Annie H. Wu, Angel M. Okoro, Doruk Savaş, Bahati C. Nkera, Ezgi Memiş, Isla A.W. Brooks, Jayden Cyrus, Chloe S. Zhao, Aastha Kumari, Pablo Iturralde, Cambria Chou-Freed, Griffin G. Hartmann, Meet Zandawala, Mustafa Talay, Gilad Barnea
abstract: Fisher et al. develop ds-Tango, a circuit-tracing tool that provides selective genetic access to the monosynaptic and disynaptic partners of a group of starter neurons. They use it to identify courtship-regulating neurons upon which sexually dimorphic olfactory circuits converge.

title: Uptake via the leaf surface allows plants to perceive volatiles with closed stomata
authors: Hao Yu, Tristan M. Cofer, Heike Lindner, Lei Wang, Antonio Aristides Pereira Gomes Filho, Sicong Zhou, Gaétan Glauser, Michael T. Raissig, James Hartwell, Jamie M. Waterman, Christelle A.M. Robert, Matthias Erb
abstract: If and how plants detect stress volatiles when their stomata are closed is unclear. Yu et al. show that the succulent CAM plant Kalanchoë laxiflora can take up herbivore-induced volatiles via the leaf surface, which enables robust volatile perception independently of stomatal opening.

title: Two ancient nuclear lineages and divergent reproductive strategies drive global success of the wheat stripe rust pathogen
authors: Jierong Wang, Yiwen Xu, Zhiru Li, Gangming Zhan, Jiasui Zhan, Zhensheng Kang, Jing Zhao
abstract: Wang et al. reveal that two ancient nuclear lineages, contrasting reproductive strategies, and recurrent nuclear exchange jointly shape the global population structure, virulence evolution, and worldwide success of the wheat stripe rust pathogen.

title: Shared texture-like representations underlie deep neural network alignment with human visual processing
authors: Jessica Loke, Lynn K.A. Sörensen, Iris I.A. Groen, Natalie Cappaert, H. Steven Scholte
abstract: Loke et al. show that DNN-brain alignment reflects a shared sensitivity to local image statistics rather than object information. Object categories are decodable from EEGs, yet alignment is strongest where object information is lowest. This dissociation shows that alignment need not imply shared obj…

title: High-precision localized feeding by blue whales
authors: John P. Ryan, Amanda I. Vanegas Ledesma, William K. Oestreich, Kelly J. Benoit-Bird, Jeremy A. Goldbogen, John Calambokidis, James A. Fahlbusch
abstract: Ryan et al. use biologging and satellite remote sensing to show how blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) can precisely and persistently localize feeding within a favorable foraging habitat by sensing and responding to thermal gradients near the ocean surface.

title: What it means to be Homo
authors: Michael Gross
abstract: A wealth of new evidence on our evolutionary ancestry makes a revision of the family tree necessary. The current delineation of the genus Homo may no longer be adequate.

title: Frankia root nodules
authors: Stefanie Kautz, Daniel J. Ballhorn
abstract: Kautz and Ballhorn introduce the process of root nodule formation following colonization by Frankia bacteria.

title: An anatomical map of squid lateral lines
authors: Haoming Wang, Carsten Wolff, Nicolas Pintozzi, Anna-Maria Petriv, Brian M. McDermott
abstract: Wang et al. map a previously unknown lateral line system across the mantle, fins, and siphon of squid paralarvae, extending far beyond the head and arm systems described to date. Hair bundles across these structures show distinct organizations, arranged as lines or fields, with length varying system…

title: Developmental mechanics: How elongating snake embryos coil to fit their space
authors: A. Richard Palmer
abstract: Spiral coiling allows elongate early snake embryos to develop within a tightly confined space. A recent survey has revealed that initial coiling is overwhelmingly dextral and arises via a quite unexpected mechanism: the linear, slower-growing, extracorporeal gut forms an elastic tether that constrai…

title: Photomorphogenesis: A molecular brake on PIF4
authors: Oihik Mitra, Enamul Huq
abstract: A new study characterizes an E3 ubiquitin ligase, LONG PETIOLE 1 (LOP1), as a missing piece in the phytochrome B (phyB)–PIF4 signaling cascade. LOP1 and phyB mutually stabilize each other and restrict PIF4 through proteasomal degradation, resulting in optimized plant growth and development.

title: Ancient mechanics: Bacterial MAIN domains reveal an evolutionary link to eukaryotic mechanotransduction
authors: Kumaran S. Ramamurthi
abstract: A newly discovered family of microbial autoproteolytic domains suggests that bacteria and animals may share a common strategy for responding to physical forces. Beyond uncovering an ancient protein fold, this work opens new questions about how microbes use mechanical cues to regulate adhesion, nutri…

title: Plant evolution: Building nodules from borrowed parts
authors: Benjamin Péret
abstract: Root nodules are distinct organs assembled from ancient developmental components. A new study shows that rhizobial Nod factors activate a conserved auxin module controlling lateral root formation, revealing how symbiotic signals can recruit pre-existing programmes without reproducing lateral root de…

title: Plant tropisms: pH-guided saprotropism enables roots to avoid decay zones
authors: Tino Colombi, Vinay Shukla, Craig Sturrock, Malcolm J. Bennett, Rahul Bhosale
abstract: Plants use tropisms, directional growth responses, to navigate diverse environmental cues such as light, gravity, water, temperature and salinity. A recent study shows roots avoid microbial decay zones by sensing pH gradients generated by decomposition, uncovering a new tropism — saprotropism.

title: Plant morphogenesis: Growth under constraint
authors: Constance Le Gloanec, Yuchen Long
abstract: The shape of growing tissues is affected by their neighbours. A new study of the gynoecium in the flower of Arabidopsis thaliana shows how mechanical coupling preserves straight organ form and may support ovule production, while unpaired mechanical constraint converts longitudinal cell elongation in…

title: Paleobiology: There’s something fishy about American ‘cheetahs’
authors: Lars Werdelin
abstract: The ‘American cheetah’ was not a cheetah at all — rather, this Pleistocene predator was closely related to pumas. A new study reveals an unknown Arctic population of this species, with an unusual penchant for fish.

title: Neuroscience: Sex shapes brain-wide sensory activity
authors: Anita V. Devineni
abstract: How widespread are sex differences in brain activity? A new study in Caenorhabditis elegans examines brain-wide responses to chemical stimuli and finds that sexually dimorphic responses are widespread and stimulus-dependent, with most sensory neurons showing both dimorphic and non-dimorphic response…

title: Oxygen in photosymbiosis evolution
authors: Loïc Quevarec, Clément Car, Gaël Brasseur, Christophe Robaglia
abstract: Although oxygen, a major product of oxygenic photosynthesis, has played a significant role in the evolution of the biosphere, its involvement in photosymbioses remains poorly understood, and this review by Quevarec et al. explores its role.

title: Growth directions and stiffness across cell layers determine whether tissues stay smooth or buckle
authors: Avilash Singh Yadav, Lilan Hong, Patrick M. Klees, Annamaria Kiss, Manuel Petit, Xi He, Iselle M. Barrios, Michelle Heeney, Anabella Maria D. Galang, Richard S. Smith, Arezki Boudaoud, Adrienne H.K. Roeder
abstract: Singh Yadav et al. show that smooth sepal morphogenesis requires aligned longitudinal growth and comparable stiffness across epidermal layers. Ectopic AS2 expression disrupts this balance, causing outer epidermal buckling. Buckling promotes PIN1 convergence at the buckle tips to initiate outgrowths,…

abstract: Leveraging the Drosophila male whole-brain connectome, Rubin et al. describe an expansive and highly intertwined male-specific network poised to control male social behaviors. They construct genetic driver lines for specific, sexually dimorphic cell types. Optogenetic manipulations reveal cell-type-…

title: Single-neuron connectome of nucleus accumbens
authors: Yuan Liu, Wei Song, Xiaoxue Shi, Qiumiao Wang, Wanqiu Zhou, Qing Li, Biyu Ren, Xueyan Jia, Xiangning Li, Hui Gong, Yan-Gang Sun, Xiaofei Wang
abstract: Liu et al. map the projectomes of NAc MSNs with single-cell resolution and identify different monosynaptic inputs to MSN populations across NAc subregions. Single-cell projectome analysis of NAc-projecting cortical and hippocampal neurons further reveals diverse collateralization and co-projection p…

title: Carotid body dysfunction contributes to respiratory instability in Rett syndrome
authors: Monica L. Strain, Eliandra N. da Silva, Michelle L. Olsen, Daniel K. Mulkey
abstract: Strain et al. demonstrate that peripheral chemoreception contributes to unstable breathing in MeCP2-deficient mice by a mechanism involving diminished dopamine signaling. Limiting peripheral chemoreception by breathing hyperoxia or augmenting dopamine signaling stabilizes breathing in MeCP2-deficien…

title: Core circadian clock genes control molecular and behavioral circatidal rhythms in Parhyale hawaiensis
authors: Victoria Louis, Zachary Bellido, Adam Helfenbein, Joshua J.C. Rosenthal, Patrick Emery
abstract: The 12.4-h circatidal clock allows marine animals to cope with the tides. Louis et al. show that in the crustacean P. hawaiensis, this timekeeper is composed of the same four core proteins as the circadian clock, but that the transcriptional wiring between these components differs in circadian and c…

title: A loss-of-function allele fixed during domestication reshapes nectar chemistry, microbial diversity, and pollinator visits
authors: Guillaume Tueux, Nicolas Pouilly, Jordan Bernigaud Samatan, Nicolas Blanchet, Marie-Claude Boniface, Olivier Catrice, Sébastien Carrère, Jérôme Gouzy, Marie-Pierre Jacquemot, Emmanuelle Lauber, Alexandra Legendre, Sandra Moreau, Marco Moroldo, Amandine Roldan, Aurélien Carlier, Nicolas B. Hexose-rich nectar attracts more bee visits and harbors less diverse fungal communities. The loss-of-function allele is rare in wild sunflowers but common in crop lines, which sugg…

title: Phosphorylation-dependent interaction between VAP proteins and INF2 influences ER morphology
authors: Frieda Kage, Miriam Lee, Siddhi Bramhe, Alastair G. McEwen, Fabien Alpy, Henry N. Higgs
abstract: Kage et al. report a novel phosphorylation-dependent interaction between INF2 and VAP proteins. Increased cytoplasmic calcium stimulates INF2 phosphorylation, which, in turn, allows VAP binding. The INF2-VAP interaction does not influence INF2-mediated actin polymerization but does play a role in ER…

title: Mechanical conflicts control fruit morphogenesis in Arabidopsis
authors: Binghan Wang, Andrea Gómez-Felipe, Amelie Bauer, Aubry Fenestre, Ayanava Giri, Richard S. Smith, Daniel Kierzkowski
abstract: Wang et al. show that mechanical conflicts from differential growth shape the Arabidopsis gynoecium and fruit. Fast-growing valves stretch the replum, amplifying elongation and ovule production. After fertilization, the replum and valve elongate more synchronously; if valves fail to expand, the repl…

title: Whole-brain chemosensory responses of both C. elegans sexes
authors: Maedeh Seyedolmohadesin, Xingyang Fu, Mahdi Torkashvand, Sina Rasouli, Samuel Lang, Liangzi Li, Cristine Kalinski, Steven J. Cook, Frank C. Schroeder, Eviatar Yemini, Vivek Venkatachalam
abstract: Seyedolmohadesin et al. record whole-brain activity with cellular resolution in both C. elegans sexes during broad chemosensory stimulation. They find that nearly every sensory neuron and many pharyngeal neurons respond in a sexually dimorphic manner and that these functional dimorphisms are distinc…

authors: Molly Cassatt-Johnstone, T. Brock Wooldridge, Sambit Ghosh, Elizabeth Hall, Susan Hewitson, Julie Meachen, Matthew J. Wooller, Grant Zazula, Beth Shapiro
abstract: Cassatt-Johnstone et al. use paleogenomics to show that extinct American cheetahs were most closely related to pumas, not cheetahs. These cats ranged far into the Arctic and exploited aquatic prey, thus fundamentally expanding our view of Pleistocene predator ecology and demonstrating the power of a…
